Yes, I've read Feast twice, and while I did enjoy it, it confirmed what I had begun to suspect as early as book 2--that the cohesion of the tale was slowly unraveling at the seams. By Feast, the story had stopped simply meandering through a large world and had stumbled off into the wilderness entirely.

In A Game of Thrones, GRRM clearly sets the stage for the story he wants to tell, and the inevitable conflicts that must take place before the series ends--that is, the coming of Winter, the invasion and defeat of the White Walkers, and in general, some resolution, good or bad, for the ruling of Westeros and for the main characters: Tyrion, Danerys, and The Starks, especially the children and Jon Snow in particular. How we get to that point is, of course, never a straight line and it does take time--it would be unsatisfying if it didn't. The worldbuilding, new characters, mysteries uncovered, shocking moments, etc. are all part of the fun and can be critical to the unveiling of the story.

But not everything that can happen in Westeros has to happen, or happen "on stage." At a certain point, another new character, another new plot line, become distractions. I would put forth that GRRM reached that point a long time ago, and the multi-year delays in finishing each successive book are either a symptom of or caused by his loss of control over the story.
